hints: Compare the melting points, 44 degrees C and 590 degrees C, and think what type of structure melts very easily and what type needs very high temperature.
Recall what separates when a simple molecule like $\text{P}_4$ melts compared with what must break when a giant network melts.
Link the low melting point to weak forces between molecules and the high melting point to strong bonds throughout a lattice.
walkthrough:
Picture the two different worlds**
Think of white phosphorus as separate little $\text{P}_4$ tetrahedra sitting next to each other in the solid. They are held to each other only by weak attractions. Red phosphorus is very different, it is one huge joined up network of P atoms linked by covalent bonds in all directions.

Name the structures correctly**
Separate molecules means simple molecular, also called simple covalent. A continuous network means giant molecular, also called giant covalent or macromolecular. So $\text{P}_4$ is simple molecular and P is giant molecular.

Explain melting at particle level**
When $\text{P}_4$ melts, you do not break any P-P covalent bonds inside the $\text{P}_4$ molecule. You only separate one $\text{P}_4$ molecule from the next, so you only overcome weak London dispersion forces, little energy needed, low melting point. When red P melts, there are no separate molecules to separate, you have to break strong P-P covalent bonds throughout the giant structure, a lot of energy needed, very high melting point.

Final answer: structure of $\text{P}_4$ : simple molecular
structure of P : giant molecular / giant covalent
Melting $\text{P}_4$ overcomes weak London dispersion forces between $\text{P}_4$ molecules, whereas melting P requires breaking strong covalent bonds in the giant lattice, so more energy is needed for red phosphorus.

hints: Use the sign of $\Delta H = -17.6 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ to decide whether the product level is above or below the $\text{P}_4$ level already drawn.
walkthrough:
Read the energy change**
$\Delta H$ is negative, so heat is given out. That means the product red P must be lower in enthalpy than the reactant white $\text{P}_4$. Draw a lower horizontal line for P, then connect the upper $\text{P}_4$ line to it with a hump showing the activation energy barrier. Label the axes enthalpy and progress of reaction.

Final answer: Exothermic pathway: horizontal level for $\text{P}_4$ higher than level for P, joined by curve with activation energy hump; y-axis labelled enthalpy, x-axis labelled progress of reaction.

hints: Let the oxidation number of P be x, take O as -2, and set the total for neutral $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ equal to zero.
walkthrough:
Balance charges to find P**
In oxides O is $-2$. For neutral $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$: $$4x + 10(-2) = 0$$ $$4x = +20$$ $$x = +5$$ So phosphorus is in oxidation state +5, its maximum for Period 3.

hints: Both $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ hydrolyse to the same phosphorus containing product, the common P(V) acid.
Balance P first, then O and H with water, remembering $\text{PCl}_5$ also produces $\text{HCl}$ and $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10}$ produces four moles of acid.
walkthrough:
Spot the common product**
P(V) chloride and P(V) oxide both hydrolyse fully to phosphoric acid, $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$. That is Q. Chloride hydrolysis also gives $\text{HCl}$ from the Cl atoms.

Balance the two equations**
For reaction 1, one P gives one $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$, five Cl give five $\text{HCl}$. Count H and O to find water: $$\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$$ For reaction 2, four P give four $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$: $$\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$ Check O: $10+6=16$ on each side, H: $12=12$.

Final answer: Q is $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$.
reaction 1: $\text{PCl}_5 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + 5\text{HCl}$
reaction 2: $\text{P}_4\text{O}_{10} + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 4\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$

hints: Count carbons and hydrogens from three $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$ rings plus one P, then check if the ratio can simplify.
walkthrough:
Add up the phenyl groups**
Each phenyl is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$. Three of them give $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{15}$, plus the central P gives $\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{15}\text{P}$. The 18:15:1 ratio has no common divisor, so molecular and empirical formulas are the same.

hints: Think what $\text{NaBH}_4$ does to the $\text{C=O}$ bond in propanal $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$.
Think what happens when an alcohol G is treated with red phosphorus and $\text{I}_2$, what group replaces the $\text{OH}$ group.
walkthrough:
Classify stage 1**
$\text{NaBH}_4$ adds hydrogen across the aldehyde $\text{C=O}$ to give a primary alcohol. Gain of hydrogen, loss of oxygen from the carbonyl, is reduction.

Classify stage 2**
G is an alcohol reacting to form $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{I}$. The $\text{OH}$ group is swapped for I using red phosphorus and $\text{I}_2$, a classic halogenation of an alcohol. One group substitutes for another, so substitution.

Final answer: stage 1: reduction
stage 2: substitution

hints: Draw G by converting $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$ with $\text{NaBH}_4$ into its primary alcohol, keep the three carbon chain.
For the Wittig step, join the aldehyde carbon of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$ to the $\text{CH}_2$ carbon of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{I}$ with a $\text{C=C}$ bond, removing O and I.
walkthrough:
Draw G**
Propanal $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$ reduced gives propan-1-ol: $$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$$ That is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.

Build the Wittig alkene H**
In the general Wittig equation $\text{R}^1\text{CHO} + \text{R}^2\text{CH}_2\text{I} \rightarrow \text{R}^1\text{CH}=\text{CHR}^2$. Here both $\text{R}^1$ and $\text{R}^2$ are $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5$. Joining the two carbons gives: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CHC}_2\text{H}_5$$ which is hex-3-ene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Final answer: G is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ (propan-1-ol)
H is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (hex-3-ene)

hints: Identify J as $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ and cut the $\text{C=C}$ bond into two carbonyl fragments.

Remember with hot concentrated acidified $\text{MnO}_4^-$, any aldehyde fragment is oxidised further to a carboxylic acid, while a disubstituted $\text{C}$ gives a ketone that resists further oxidation.
walkthrough:
Split the double bond**
J is 2-methylpent-2-ene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Hot concentrated $\text{MnO}_4^-$ in acid cleaves the $\text{C=C}$ completely. The left side $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=$ becomes propanone, $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$, a ketone which is stable to further oxidation.

Oxidise the aldehyde fragment fully**
The right side $=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ would first give propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$, but under hot concentrated conditions it is oxidised straight on to propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ (propanoic acid) and $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$ (propanone)
